newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Anglo seen big winner from Lonrho/JCI link.
newsitem.headline: Anglo seen big winner from Lonrho/JCI link.

text.p: A merger between JCI Ltd and Lonrho Plc would create one of the world's biggest mining houses but the ultimate winner could be Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd, analysts said on Monday.

JCI, South Africa's sixth-largest mining house, and Lonrho confirmed on Monday they were in talks on a possible merger which would create a global miner with a market capitalisation estimated at more than $3 billion.
Analysts said they believed the merger was initiated by Anglo, which was forced last month by the European Commission to cut its 27.5 percent stake in Lonrho to 9.99 percent over the next two years.
The Commission said Anglo platinum interests combined with that of Lonrho would put control of the world's platinum industry in the hands of Anglo and another South African company, Gencor Ltd.
"Anglo still desires control. By initiating a Lonrho (merger with) JCI, Anglo gets diluted in Lonrho -- so that it gets out of its selling problem.
"It is a nice situation for Anglo," Investec Securities analyst John Clemmow said.
Anglo has made no secret that its principal interest in Lonrho is the company's stake in Ghana's Ashanti Gold Fields Co Ltd, one of Africa's most succesful gold mining firms.
Anglo director Michael Spicer declined to comment: "We are not going to comment on market speculation."
Analysts said a merger between JCI, the first South African mining house under black control, and Lonrho was first discussed last year by the two companies' management.

A merger would make good business sense, not least in the coal arena where the combined company could add Lonrho's Duiker Mining Ltd to its Tavistock division, recently enlarged with the acquisition of Royal Dutch/Shell's South African coal business.
But any tie-up would be littered with complications.
"It all sounds good on paper but there are a lot of complications still," Barnard, Jacobs and Mellet analyst Robinn Kearney said.

The Financial Times on Monday quoted Ken Costa, vice chairman of investment bank SBC Warburg -- an adviser to both JCI and Anglo -- as saying any merger would have to happen rapidly to quash market speculation.

"The commercial logic of the transaction is compelling and di3cussions to establish merger terms that are fair to both sides will need to happen rapidly in order to avoid unnecessary speculation in the financial markets," Costa said.
JCI was taken over by black businessman Mzi Khumalo's African Mining Group earlier this year in a deal worth 2.4 billion rand.
Britain's Sunday Telegraph said that under the proposals Lonrho would bid for JCI, which is valued at 900 million pounds, and the new company would be listed in London and Johannesburg.
The newspaper said the plan envisaged Anglo American swapping its 27.5 percent stake in Lonrho, plus some cash, for Lonrho's 41 percent in Ashanti.
Clemmow said a merger would be of significant benefit to JCI, a company with few foreign assets.
"It looks a company that needs a big deal."
